(b) Find the cheapest whole-number plan. \(x =\) [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] \(y =\) [[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]]

[[feedback:prt2]]

(c) The least cost is Ksh [[input:ans4]] [[validation:ans4]] [[feedback:prt3]]

generalfeedback.text:
(a) \({@ta1@}\). The other conditions are \(y \le {@YY@}\), \(x + y \le {@NN@}\), \(x \ge 0\), \(y \ge 0\).

(b) The cheapest corner of R for \(C = {@cx@}x + {@cy@}y\) is \({@vd@}\), which is not a whole-number point. With an ‘at least’ condition, round up and check: the cheapest whole-number plan is \(x = {@bst[1]@}\), \(y = {@bst[2]@}\).

(c) \(C = {@cx@} \times {@bst[1]@} + {@cy@} \times {@bst[2]@} = {@t@}\): Ksh \({@thou(t)@}\).

questiondescription.text:
Linear Programming: minimum cost

Grade 12 CBE Core 1.4 (d) / Essential 1.4 (d): Write an at-least requirement as an inequality and find the cheapest whole-number plan of stores within the limits, and its cost.

Core and Essential

This question is adapted from Chapter 8, Sections 2.1 and 2.2 of School Mathematics Project, SMP Book 5 (Metric), ed. P. G. Bowie, Cambridge University Press, 1969: the least-cost way to cover an at-least amount with two sizes, a limit on the large size and on the total; set as hiring stores rather than B5's lorries, with Kenyan contexts and new capacities and costs.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Core and Essential Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

feedbackvariables.text: k1: lcls(ans1, ta1); w1: lcls(ans1, sw1);

truefeedback.text: Your inequality says there is room for \({@RR@}\) {@un@} or less. ‘At least \({@RR@}\)’ means the room cannot go below \({@RR@}\).
You matched the capacities to the wrong letters: \(x\) counts the stores that hold \({@ca@}\) {@un@}.

falsefeedback.text: Amount stored = (capacity of one) \(\times\, x\) + (capacity of the other) \(\times\, y\), and it must be at least \({@RR@}\).

feedbackvariables.text: enough: is(ca*ans2 + cb*ans3 >= RR); lim: is(ans3 <= YY and ans2 + ans3 <= NN and ans2 >= 0 and ans3 >= 0);

truefeedback.text: You rounded down: then there is room for only \({@ca*dn[1]+cb*dn[2]@}\) {@un@}, less than \({@RR@}\). With an ‘at least’ condition, round up.

falsefeedback.text: Your plan has room for only \({@ca*ans2+cb*ans3@}\) {@un@}, less than \({@RR@}\).

[[if test='is(ans2 < 0 or ans3 < 0)']]

The numbers hired cannot be negative.

[[else]][[if test='is(ans3 > YY)']]

Your plan hires \({@ans3@}\) {@lg@}, but only \({@YY@}\) are free.

[[/if]][[if test='is(ans2 + ans3 > NN)']]

Your plan hires \({@ans2 + ans3@}\) altogether, but the limit is \({@NN@}\).

[[/if]][[/if]]

truefeedback.text: That is the most expensive plan, Ksh \({@thou(tw)@}\).

falsefeedback.text: Your plan works but costs Ksh \({@thou(Cof(ans2, ans3))@}\); another plan near the corner costs less.

truefeedback.text: That is the cost at the corner of R, which is not a whole-number plan.
That is the cost of your plan in (b), but your plan is not the cheapest.

falsefeedback.text: That is not the cost of your plan in (b), which is \({@cx@} \times {@ans2@} + {@cy@} \times {@ans3@}\). Work it out again, and check that your plan is the cheapest one.
